title: Checkpoint: A Structure Is a Promise You Must Be Able to Prove
summary: This checkpoint week revisits the hardest ideas of the cross-border phase and ends with a mock defence of a hypothetical structure chart. The central idea is that every box and arrow on a chart is a claim about where decisions are made, where profit belongs and how money moves. A structure that cannot evidence its claims is a liability, however good it looks.
body:
A structure chart is not a picture of your companies. It is a set of claims: that each entity is resident where it says, earns what it says, pays what it says and moves money the way the arrows say. This week you prove you can defend every one of those claims out loud.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between an asset sale and a share sale?

A. An asset sale sells the property, so the owning company realises the gain and any recapture, and the buyer gets a fresh tax cost. A share sale sells the company, so the property keeps its old tax cost and the buyer inherits the latent tax.

Q. What are the three gates cross-border money must pass?

A. Registration with the state where required, permission to convert and remit, and a bank willing to carry the money under its know-your-customer duties.

Q. What does a tax treaty do?

A. It allocates taxing rights between two countries, sets limits on source taxation such as withholding rates, resolves dual residence through tie-breaker rules, and provides relief from double tax by credit or exemption.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the cross-border phase covered eleven weeks: structure as design, residence and substance, treaties, repatriation, foreign affiliates, financing the structure, transfer pricing, indirect taxes, moving money and exit tax. Each was taught as its own subject. In practice they arrive together, in one meeting, from one hostile reader: a tax auditor who wants to reallocate profit, or a banker who wants to know whether the money can reach the loan. This week rebuilds the phase as a single defence. On Day 6 you will sit through a full mock meeting with both.

The chart is a list of claims

In plain English: every line on your chart says something that someone may ask you to prove.

The professional framing is that a structure has three layers, and a hostile reader tests each. The legal layer: which entities exist, who owns them, who controls them. The tax layer: where each entity is resident, what profit it earns, what it pays to others, at what price, and what each payment attracts in withholding. The money layer: which accounts, currencies and approvals carry each flow. A chart that shows only the legal layer invites the reader to fill in the other two for you, and they will fill them in unfavourably.

A worked example, hypothetical. A chart shows an individual owning a holding company in country A, which owns a project company in country B. The arrows show a management fee from B to A, an intercompany loan from A to B, and dividends from B to A. Each arrow is a claim. The fee claims A really provides services worth its price. The loan claims the debt is genuine, priced at arm's length and within any thin-capitalisation limit. The dividend claims B has paid its tax and that withholding was applied at the right rate under the treaty. And the box marked A claims A is resident in A, which is only true if its real decisions are made there. Four arrows and two boxes; six things to prove.

The three ideas that carry the phase

First, substance follows the decision-maker. Residence and permanent establishment are decided by where real decisions and real activity happen, not by where documents are filed. Second, form must match flow. A fee, a loan, a dividend and a return of capital move money in the same direction and are taxed completely differently, so each payment's legal form must be real, documented and priced at arm's length. Third, money must be able to move. A structure that is tax-efficient and lawful but cannot clear a bank, a central bank or a registration requirement is not a working structure.

Say that out loud now.

Substance follows the decision-maker. Form must match flow. Money must be able to move.

Testing the chart against all three

A second worked example, hypothetical, using the same chart. Substance: the holding company's two directors live in country B and decide everything by phone from there, and the board meets in A once a year to sign. Its residence claim in A is weak. Form: the management fee is 5 percent of revenue, set by habit, with no service agreement or record of services. Its arm's length claim is weak. Money: the loan from A to B was never registered with B's central bank, where registration is required to protect repayment. Its repayment claim is weak. Three weaknesses, and every one of them is a documentation and decision-making failure, not a tax-rate problem. Fixing them costs a few board meetings held where they should be, a service agreement and a filing.

How the best do it

Disciplined international groups keep what is often called a structure book: one document per entity recording its purpose, residence basis, directors, decisions taken and where, intercompany agreements with their pricing basis, bank accounts and registrations. It is updated as things change, not rebuilt when an auditor calls. A small developer can copy it with one page per entity and a habit of updating that page after every board meeting.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: each arrow must carry the form, price and withholding it claims. Liability: each box must be a real entity with its own decisions, or limited liability can be challenged. Banking: each flow must clear the three gates. Governance: each decision must be taken by the right people in the right place and minuted. Estate: the individual at the top needs a plan that matches how the chart holds the assets. Exit: the chart must leave a sale form open that a buyer will accept and that is taxed as modelled.

Professional sign-off required: tax advisers and corporate lawyers in each country on the chart.

The phase as one sequence

Put the eleven weeks back in the order a real structure is built, because the order is part of the lesson. First, the six lenses and the flow of funds, Week 55. Then residence and substance, because every box depends on it, Week 56. Then treaties, which only help an entity that is genuinely resident and the real owner of its income, Week 57. Then the form of each payment upward and its withholding, Week 58, and the controlled-foreign-company logic that may tax passive income at home anyway, Week 59. Then how the structure is financed and how intercompany prices are set, Weeks 60 and 61. Then the indirect taxes on what the project buys and sells, Week 62. Then whether money can physically move, Week 63, and finally how the whole thing is taxed when you leave it, Week 64.

Read that sequence as a checklist. A structure that skips a step does not fail at that step; it fails later, at the step that depended on it. A treaty claim fails because residence failed. An exit fails because the holding structure was chosen without one. Each later week inherits the weaknesses of every earlier one, which is why this checkpoint revisits them together.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a chart that is designed well and operated badly, so every claim is plausible on paper and unprovable in practice. The control is the structure book, kept current, and an annual self-audit of every box and arrow against it.

The beginner's mistake

Defending a structure by its tax result. An auditor does not care what it saves; she cares whether it is real. Defend it by its evidence.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught that avoidance and evasion are separated by substance over form and by honest disclosure, and that anti-avoidance rules can recharacterise arrangements without real purpose. Every claim on this week's chart is tested against that line. A structure that would survive only if nobody looked is already on the wrong side of it.

Recap

A structure chart is a list of claims across three layers: legal, tax and money. Three ideas carry the phase: substance follows the decision-maker, form must match flow, and money must be able to move. Keep a structure book and audit every box and arrow against it.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Fundy Settlement case, and an offshore trust whose real decisions were made at home.
checklist: I can state the claim behind every box and arrow on my chart.
I keep a structure book with one page per entity.
Each entity's decisions are taken and minuted where it claims residence.
Every intercompany payment has a written agreement and pricing basis.
Every flow on the chart clears registration, conversion and a bank.
I can name the withholding on every cross-border payment.
I audit my own structure once a year against the structure book.
I defend my structure by its evidence, not its tax result.
head: Field checklist
speak: A structure chart is not a picture of companies; it is a list of claims. Each box claims residence and real decisions. Each arrow, a fee, a loan, a dividend or a return of capital, claims a legal form, an arm's length price and the right withholding. And each flow claims it can pass registration, currency rules and a bank. Three ideas carry the whole phase. Substance follows the decision-maker: residence sits where real decisions are made. Form must match flow: each payment must really be what it says and be priced fairly. And money must be able to move. A chart that is well designed but badly operated, with directors deciding from the wrong country, fees with no agreement and unregistered loans, fails on evidence, not on tax rates. So I keep a structure book with a page per entity, update it after every board meeting, and audit every box and arrow once a year.
terms: Structure book — a record, kept per entity, of purpose, residence basis, directors, decisions, intercompany agreements, accounts and registrations.
Claim — a statement a structure makes about residence, form, price or movement of money that a reviewer may require you to prove.
Self-audit — a periodic review of your own structure against its evidence, done before an external reviewer does it.

hostile.q: Your chart says the holding company is resident in country A. Prove it.
hostile.a: Here is its structure book page. Its board has a majority of directors resident in A, it met in A four times last year, and the minutes show the decisions taken at those meetings: approving the budget, the loan to the project company and the distribution. The papers were circulated in advance and the directors deliberated. Here are the meeting locations, the attendance and the decisions. If any of that changes, the page changes with it.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole on audit and integrity
title: Fundy Settlement: An Offshore Trust Run from Home
summary: Trusts set up with a Barbados trustee sold shares at a large gain and claimed treaty protection. Canada's courts, ending with the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012, held that the trusts were resident in Canada because their real decisions were made there by the beneficiaries, not by the offshore trustee. The lesson is that residence follows where decisions are actually made.
body:
A structure can be correctly formed, correctly registered and correctly documented, and still fail, because the documents say decisions were made offshore and the evidence says they were made at home. Fundy Settlement is the clearest example of that gap in recent Canadian law.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the composite exit case, and what is Rule 64?

A. The exit was designed at the exit, with the price agreed before the form of sale and its tax. Rule 64: never agree a price until the form of sale, its tax in a current written opinion, and who bears every tax are fixed in writing.

Q. What was the root cause for those exposed in Argentina 2001 to 2002?

A. Treating a currency peg and access to bank deposits as fixed facts rather than as policies that could be withdrawn, which left currency mismatches unpriced.

Q. What is beneficial ownership in a treaty context?

A. The requirement, in many treaties, that the person claiming reduced withholding is the true owner of the income, with the right to use and enjoy it, not a conduit passing it on to someone else.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this case is about evidence, and evidence is Cole's subject. It is a real case. I will keep to the facts I am confident of and leave out figures I cannot vouch for. The decision is the Supreme Court of Canada's 2012 judgment in the matter usually called Fundy Settlement, also known by the name of its trustee, St. Michael Trust Corp.; read the judgment itself before relying on any detail, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. For a developer building cross-border holdings, it is the case that explains why your offshore entity is only as offshore as the people who actually run it.

1. Timeline

In the late 1990s, members of a Canadian family arranged a reorganisation in which interests in a Canadian business came to be held by trusts. The trusts were settled with a trust company resident in Barbados as trustee. The beneficiaries were Canadian residents. Later, the trusts sold shares at a large gain and claimed that, as Barbados residents, they were protected from Canadian tax on that gain by the Canada and Barbados tax treaty. The Canadian tax authority assessed the trusts as Canadian residents. The Tax Court of Canada agreed with the authority, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and in 2012 the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the trusts' appeal.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choice was the governance model. The structure placed legal trusteeship in Barbados while leaving the people with the real knowledge, interest and influence, the Canadian beneficiaries, in Canada. The second decision was operational: the way the trustee actually behaved, which the courts found was largely to follow the beneficiaries' wishes rather than to exercise independent judgment.

3. Assumptions

The structure rested on the assumption that a trust resides where its trustee resides, because the trustee holds legal title and signs the documents. The Supreme Court held instead that a trust's residence is determined by where its central management and control is actually exercised, the same test long used for companies. Where the trustee merely carries out decisions made by others, residence follows those others.

4. Incentives

The family had an incentive to keep control of the decisions that mattered to them. The offshore trustee had an incentive to retain the business and to provide services efficiently, which in practice meant doing what the people behind the trust wanted. Neither incentive is improper. Together, they produce exactly the pattern that defeats an offshore residence claim: formal authority in one country and real authority in another.

5. Warning signs ignored

Cole's list, framed generally because I will not invent the record: any time the offshore party's role was limited to administration and signature; any time significant decisions were discussed and settled onshore before reaching the trustee; any time the trustee's agreement was assumed rather than sought. Each of those leaves a trail in emails, meeting notes and advisers' files. An auditor reads that trail, and the courts did.

Say that out loud now.

Residence follows the decision-maker, not the signature.

6. Point of no return

For a structure like this, the point of no return is usually not the sale. It is the long period before it, during which the pattern of who actually decides is laid down. By the time a large gain is realised, the evidence of where management and control sat has already been written, day by day, in ordinary correspondence. It cannot be rewritten afterwards without making things much worse.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a gap between formal and real authority: a structure that relied on residence while the substance of decision-making stayed where it started. Clever documents cannot close that gap. Only real decisions, taken by real people, in the place the structure claims, can.

The prevention rule

Rule 65: Never claim an entity is resident or managed anywhere I am not prepared to put real decision-makers, with real judgment, and the record to prove it; if the decisions stay with me, the residence stays with me too.

What a developer should take from it

A worked illustration, hypothetical. A developer forms a holding company in a low-tax country to own project companies elsewhere, with two local directors provided by a services firm. If every acquisition, loan and distribution is decided by the developer in his home country and then sent to the directors to sign, the holding company's claim to be resident and managed abroad is weak, whatever its documents say. If instead the board receives papers in advance, debates them, sometimes asks for changes, and records those discussions at meetings held where it claims residence, the claim has substance. The cost of the second model is real: directors with genuine competence, real meetings, and the developer giving up some control. That cost is the price of the residence claim. If it is not worth paying, the claim is not worth making.

Cole's evidence test

Cole's practical test for any entity that claims to be managed somewhere other than where its owner lives is to ask for three documents from the last year. The board papers for one significant decision, with the date they were sent. The minutes of the meeting that took it, with who attended and where. And the correspondence between the owner and the directors in the week before. If the papers arrived the day of the meeting, the minutes record only a resolution, and the correspondence shows the owner telling the directors what to do, the residence claim is already lost; the court case would only confirm it. If the papers arrived in good time, the minutes show questions, and the correspondence shows the owner recommending rather than instructing, the claim has a foundation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing that formation and documents settle residence, so that day-to-day conduct quietly undermines the structure. The control is a substance record and a governance practice that puts real decisions where the structure says they are. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in each country on residence, and trust or corporate counsel on governance.

The beginner's mistake

Sending offshore directors an email that says "please sign the attached by Friday". That single sentence, repeated over years, is evidence of where management and control really sits.

Callback

In Week 56, Elias and Ford taught residence and substance, mind and management, and the habit of a substance record. Fundy Settlement is that lesson tested at the highest court, with a large gain at stake. In Week 21, LEX taught that limited liability can be challenged when an entity is a mere instrument; residence fails for the same reason, from the tax side.

Recap

Trusts with a Barbados trustee sold shares at a large gain and claimed treaty protection. The Supreme Court of Canada, in 2012, held they were resident in Canada because central management and control was exercised there, by the beneficiaries, not by the trustee. Rule 65: never claim residence where I will not put real decision-makers and the record to prove it.

Next: Roman on The Money: how a banker reads a cross-border structure chart.
checklist: I know who actually makes each entity's significant decisions.
Decision-makers sit where each entity claims residence.
Board papers go out in advance and directors genuinely deliberate.
Minutes record discussion, not only resolutions.
I never send directors documents with an instruction simply to sign.
I keep a substance record for every offshore entity.
I have written residence advice from a tax adviser in each country.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 65: Never claim an entity is resident or managed anywhere I am not prepared to put real decision-makers, with real judgment, and the record to prove it; if the decisions stay with me, the residence stays with me too.
speak: Fundy Settlement is a real Canadian case decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012. Trusts were set up with a trust company in Barbados as trustee, for Canadian beneficiaries. The trusts later sold shares at a large gain and claimed treaty protection as Barbados residents. The courts held that a trust is resident where its central management and control is actually exercised, not simply where its trustee is, and found that the real decisions were made in Canada by the beneficiaries, with the trustee largely following their wishes. So the trusts were resident in Canada. The lesson for a developer is that an offshore entity is only as offshore as the people who actually run it. Formation and documents do not settle residence; day-to-day conduct does. My rule is Rule 65: never claim residence where I will not put real decision-makers with real judgment and the record to prove it.
terms: Central management and control — the test that places residence where an entity's high-level decisions are actually made.
Trustee — the person or company that holds legal title to trust property and must manage it for the beneficiaries.
Formal versus real authority — the gap between who signs and who actually decides, which residence tests look through.

hostile.q: Your holding company's directors are provided by a services firm and you are its only shareholder. Who really decides?
hostile.a: The board decides, and here is how you can tell. Papers reach the directors a week before each meeting, they meet in person where the company is resident, and the minutes record questions, conditions and in one case a refusal of a proposal I made. I make recommendations as shareholder; they decide as directors. If the record ever stops showing that, the residence claim stops being true, and I would rather change the structure than pretend.

title: How a Banker Reads Your Structure Chart
summary: A lender reads a structure chart for one thing: whether cash from the building reliably reaches the loan, and whether anything can trap, divert or tax it first. Withholding, intercompany debt, currency gates and tax exposure all reduce the cash the lender can count. Show the lender the chain of cash, not just the chain of ownership.
body:
A tax auditor reads your chart to find profit in the wrong place. A banker reads it to find cash in the wrong place: cash that is trapped, taxed or claimed before it reaches the loan. Prepare for both readings, because they ask different questions about the same arrows.

Recall

Q. What is the latent tax discount?

A. The price reduction a share buyer asks for to reflect the tax it inherits inside the company, because it takes over the company's low tax cost in the property.

Q. What are the three leaks on a cross-border transfer?

A. The exchange spread, the transaction fees including intermediary banks, and the cost of delay.

Q. What is the difference between the credit method and the exemption method of relieving double tax?

A. Under the credit method, the residence country taxes the income and allows a credit for foreign tax paid, usually capped at its own tax on that income. Under the exemption method, the residence country does not tax the foreign income at all, sometimes taking it into account in setting the rate on other income.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in this phase you learned to design a structure that is tax-efficient and defensible. A lender will lend to that structure only if the cash it depends on can be traced, counted and protected. Many cross-border deals that pass the tax review fail the credit review, because the structure that minimises tax maximises the number of places cash can get stuck. Hypothetical numbers throughout, with assumed rates for teaching only; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The banker's question: where does my cash come from?

In plain English: the lender wants to know how many steps lie between the rent and its loan payment, and what can go wrong at each step.

The professional framing is structural subordination: when a loan is made to a holding company rather than to the company that owns the building, the holding company's lender is paid only after the project company's own creditors, its tax, its own lenders and any withholding on distributions. The holding company's lender stands behind everyone inside the project company. That is why most real estate lenders lend directly to the company that owns the property and takes security over it, and why they look so hard at any loan made higher up the chart.

A worked example, hypothetical. A project company earns net operating income of 2,000,000 dollars. A lender to the project company, with security on the building, looks at that 2,000,000 against its debt service of 1,500,000: a debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of about 1.33, which may meet a typical covenant; covenant levels are commercial practice, not standards. Now suppose instead the loan sits at the holding company in another country. The project company first pays local tax, assume 400,000 dollars, then an intercompany management fee, assume 200,000, then distributes the rest, 1,400,000, subject to withholding at an assumed 10 percent, 140,000. The holding company receives about 1,260,000 to meet 1,500,000 of debt service: coverage of 0.84. Same building, same loan; one structure services it and the other does not.

Say that out loud now.

A lender stands behind everything inside the company it does not lend to. Lend where the cash is.

What a banker subtracts

Beyond tax and withholding, a banker subtracts anything that can claim cash ahead of it. Intercompany debt: if the project company owes a shareholder loan, the lender will require it to be subordinated in writing, so the shareholder cannot be repaid while the bank is owed. Intercompany fees: the lender will often cap them or subordinate them, because a fee can drain cash before debt service. Currency gates: if the loan is in dollars and the income in local currency, the lender will test coverage at a weaker exchange rate and ask what happens if conversion is delayed. And tax exposure: if an auditor could reallocate profit or disallow interest under thin-capitalisation or transfer-pricing rules, the resulting tax is a claim on cash that ranks ahead of distributions.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The same project company with debt service of 1,500,000 also pays its shareholder 300,000 of interest on an intercompany loan. If an auditor disallows that interest as excessive under a thin-capitalisation rule, the project company's taxable income rises by 300,000, and at an assumed 25 percent its tax rises by 75,000. Coverage on the bank loan barely moves, about 1.33 to 1.28 if the extra tax is paid from income, but if the shareholder interest is not subordinated, the 300,000 paid upward is cash the bank never sees. The lender will insist on subordination precisely because of that line.

Presenting the chain of cash

Give the lender a second chart beside the ownership chart: a cash waterfall from rent to loan payment, showing each deduction in order, its legal basis, and who controls it. Mark every intercompany payment and state whether it is subordinated. Show coverage at the base exchange rate and at a weaker one. A lender who sees that you have already read your structure the way it will read it usually needs fewer conditions to lend.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet: the value of an interest in a cross-border structure is the cash it can deliver to you, after every layer of tax, withholding, fee and gate, not the value of the building at the bottom. Record your holdings at that delivered value, and note beside each the layer most likely to trap cash. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of it.

Working with advisers

This month's thread. Your tax adviser optimises for tax, your lender's counsel for security, your corporate lawyer for clean documents. Nobody but you is responsible for making them agree. Before finalising a structure, put the three in one meeting with the cash waterfall on the table and ask each one: "What in this chart do you need changed, and what does that change cost the others?"

Then write the answers down and decide. An adviser's job is to advise within their scope; yours is to choose across all of them. The structure that is perfect for one adviser and unacceptable to another is the one that fails at closing.

What a lender will ask for in writing

Expect the credit committee to ask for a short list of documents beyond the chart and the waterfall: the subordination agreement for every intercompany loan; the services agreement with its fee cap; a tax opinion or summary on withholding for any payments the lender's own cash flow depends on; confirmation that any required registration of foreign capital or debt has been filed; and a currency sensitivity on coverage. Have them ready before the first meeting. A lender that receives them unprompted reads the borrower as a professional; a lender that has to chase them reads the structure as a risk to be priced.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is designing for tax alone and discovering at credit review that the loan sits behind tax, fees and withholding the lender will not accept. The control is to model the cash waterfall and lender coverage alongside the tax result before the structure is fixed.

The beginner's mistake

Presenting the lender with an ownership chart and expecting it to work out the cash. It will, conservatively.

Callback

In Week 36, Priya taught that a loan is sized to its binding limit, whether coverage, debt yield or loan to value. This lesson adds the structure: the coverage that binds is measured where the loan sits, and every layer between the building and that point reduces it.

Recap

A banker reads your chart for the chain of cash. Lending above the property company means standing behind tax, fees, intercompany debt and withholding. Subordinate intercompany debt, cap fees, test coverage at a weaker currency and present a cash waterfall beside the ownership chart.

Next: Elias on The Rules: the phase's hardest rules revisited, with a Canada and Guyana comparison.
checklist: I show lenders a cash waterfall beside the ownership chart.
I know where the loan sits and what ranks ahead of it.
Intercompany loans are subordinated to bank debt in writing.
Intercompany fees are capped or subordinated where the lender requires.
I test coverage at a weaker exchange rate.
I model tax exposure from thin-capitalisation and transfer-pricing challenges.
I put my tax adviser, lender's counsel and corporate lawyer in one meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: A banker reads my structure chart for the chain of cash. If the loan sits at the project company that owns the building, the lender looks at the building's income against debt service. If it sits higher, at a holding company, the lender stands behind everything inside the project company: its local tax, its fees, any intercompany debt and withholding on distributions. Hypothetically, two million of income against one and a half million of debt service is coverage of about 1.33 at the project company, but after tax, a fee and withholding the holding company might receive only about 1.26 million, coverage below one. So lenders lend where the cash is, require intercompany loans to be subordinated in writing, cap fees, and test coverage at a weaker exchange rate. I present a cash waterfall beside the ownership chart, so the lender sees I have already read my structure the way it will.
terms: Structural subordination — the position of a lender to a holding company, which is paid only after the subsidiary's own creditors, taxes and withholding.
Subordination agreement — a written agreement that a junior creditor, such as a shareholder lender, will not be paid until a senior creditor is.
Cash waterfall — the ordered sequence of payments from income to the final recipient, showing each deduction.

hostile.q: Your shareholder loan to the project company is paid 300,000 dollars a year. Why should that rank ahead of my debt service?
hostile.a: It should not, and it will not. The shareholder loan will be subordinated to your loan by a written agreement: no interest or principal is paid upward while any amount is owed to you or any covenant is breached. I have also capped the management fee and subordinated it on the same terms. Your coverage is measured on income before either payment.

title: The Five Rules an Auditor Will Test First
summary: An auditor reviewing a cross-border structure tests a predictable set of rules: residence, permanent establishment, treaty entitlement and beneficial ownership, transfer pricing, and interest limits. Each turns on evidence about what really happened. Knowing the five lets you prepare the evidence before the questions arrive.
body:
A tax auditor reviewing a cross-border structure does not start from scratch. She tests five rules, usually in roughly the same order, and each one turns on evidence of what actually happened. Know the five and you know what to have ready.

Recall

Q. What is a clearance certificate?

A. A tax authority's confirmation that a non-resident seller's tax on a disposal is paid or secured, which releases the buyer from an obligation to withhold part of the price.

Q. What does anti-money-laundering law require a bank to know about you?

A. Your identity, your beneficial owners down to the individuals, the source of your funds and the purpose of your transactions, and it can require the bank to report suspicions without telling you.

Q. What is a treaty tie-breaker for a company?

A. A rule deciding which country a dual-resident company is resident in for treaty purposes, traditionally by place of effective management, and in many newer treaties by agreement between the two tax authorities.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on Day 6 you will defend a structure chart to a mock auditor. Her questions will follow these five rules. This lesson is the map of her questions. Nothing here is a jurisdictional conclusion; the tests and their details vary by country and treaty, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Rule one: residence

The auditor asks where each entity is really resident. For companies and trusts, many countries look to where central management and control, or effective management, is exercised, as Fundy Settlement showed. Evidence: board composition, meeting locations, papers, minutes and correspondence. Her favourite document is the email that tells directors what to sign.

Rule two: permanent establishment

The auditor asks whether a foreign entity has a taxable presence in her country through a fixed place of business or a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts. Evidence: offices used, people on the ground, who signs contracts locally. A developer's foreign holding company with no presence of its own can still create one if its executives run the project from a local site office and sign there.

Rule three: treaty entitlement and beneficial ownership

The auditor asks whether the entity claiming reduced withholding under a treaty is entitled to it: is it resident in the treaty country, is it the beneficial owner of the income rather than a conduit, and does it pass any anti-abuse test? Many treaties now include a principal purpose test, denying benefits where obtaining them was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement, unless granting them is in line with the treaty's object and purpose [unverified — confirm independently]. Evidence: the entity's real activity, what it does with the income it receives, and the reasons recorded for the structure at the time.

Say that out loud now.

Residence, permanent establishment, treaty entitlement, transfer pricing and interest limits: five rules, each decided by evidence.

Rule four: transfer pricing

The auditor asks whether each intercompany price is at arm's length: management fees, interest rates, guarantee fees, development fees. Evidence: written agreements made before the service, records of the services actually delivered, and a contemporaneous analysis of functions, assets, risks and comparables. A worked example, hypothetical. A project company pays a related holding company a fee of 5 percent of construction cost, 1,000,000 dollars on a 20,000,000 dollar project, with no agreement and no record of services. The auditor disallows the deduction; at an assumed tax rate of 25 percent, 250,000 dollars of tax arises in the project's country, possibly with penalties, while the holding company may already have paid tax on the same fee in its own country. Double tax on 1,000,000 dollars of income that may have been perfectly real but was never evidenced.

Rule five: interest limits

The auditor asks whether interest deductions on intercompany debt are limited, by a thin-capitalisation rule restricting debt relative to equity, by an earnings-based limit capping net interest as a share of a measure of earnings, or by recharacterising excessive debt as equity [unverified — confirm independently]. A second worked example, hypothetical. A project company has equity of 2,000,000 dollars and a related-party loan of 10,000,000. If the local rule allowed related-party debt of, say, 3 times equity, only 6,000,000 of the loan would carry deductible interest. At an assumed 8 percent, 320,000 dollars of the 800,000 dollars of interest would be non-deductible, and at an assumed 25 percent tax rate, about 80,000 dollars of extra tax a year. The ratio here is an illustrative assumption, not any country's rule.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source in both countries. Canada taxes resident companies and trusts on worldwide income, uses central management and control as a residence test alongside incorporation rules for companies, has detailed transfer-pricing rules requiring contemporaneous documentation, and limits interest through a thin-capitalisation rule and, more recently, an earnings-based interest limit for many taxpayers [unverified — confirm independently]. Guyana also taxes on a residence basis, applies withholding on certain payments to non-residents, and its treaty network is smaller than Canada's, so whether a treaty applies at all is the first question in any Guyana structure [unverified — confirm independently]. The habit in both is identical: identify each of the five rules, find the evidence it demands, and hold that evidence before the auditor asks.

Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser licensed in each country on residence, treaty entitlement, transfer pricing and interest limits.

The evidence file in practice

Build the file as a simple table with five rows and three columns for each entity: the rule, the claim the structure makes under it, and the documents that prove the claim. For residence: "managed in country A"; board composition, meeting log, minutes. For permanent establishment: "no taxable presence in country B"; office leases, staff locations, who signs contracts. For treaty entitlement: "entitled to reduced withholding"; residence certificate, beneficial-ownership analysis, the recorded reasons for the structure. For transfer pricing: "fees and interest at arm's length"; agreements, service records, benchmarking. For interest limits: "within the applicable limit"; the calculation and the advice. Update it after every year-end. A file that takes an hour to assemble from what you already hold is a file that wins audits; a file that needs to be created when the audit letter arrives is evidence of the opposite.

A worked illustration of the dependency, hypothetical. Suppose the residence row for a holding company is weak because its directors decide from the owner's home country. Then the treaty row fails too, because a company that is not resident in the treaty country cannot claim the treaty's reduced withholding. A dividend that was meant to bear 5 percent withholding may then bear the full domestic rate instead, assume 15 percent, on every distribution for every open year. One weak row has repriced every payment the structure makes. That is why residence evidence comes first in the file and first in the auditor's questions.

Then ask one more question of every row: if this claim failed, which other rows would fail with it? Residence usually sits under treaty entitlement, and transfer pricing under interest limits. Strengthen the rows other rows depend on first.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is preparing for the tax rate and not for the evidence. Every one of the five rules is decided by documents and conduct, not by the statutory rate. The control is a five-row evidence file per entity, reviewed annually.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming a treaty applies because the two countries have one. Entitlement depends on residence, beneficial ownership and anti-abuse tests, each of which must be met and evidenced.

Callback

In Week 61, Cole taught transfer pricing as arm's length plus documentation, and in Week 60 Omar and Nadia taught documented intercompany loans and thin capitalisation. This lesson places them in the auditor's order of questions, alongside residence and treaty entitlement from Weeks 56 and 57.

Recap

An auditor tests five rules: residence, permanent establishment, treaty entitlement and beneficial ownership, transfer pricing, and interest limits. Each is decided by evidence of what really happened. Keep a five-row evidence file per entity and review it every year.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: tracing a dollar of profit through the whole structure.
checklist: I keep a five-row evidence file for every entity.
Residence evidence includes board composition, locations and minutes.
I know whether any foreign entity has a permanent establishment risk.
I have checked treaty entitlement, beneficial ownership and anti-abuse tests.
Every intercompany price has a written agreement and an arm's length analysis.
I know the interest limits that apply to every intercompany loan.
I first confirm whether a treaty applies at all.
head: Field checklist
speak: A tax auditor reviewing a cross-border structure tests five rules. Residence: where each entity's real management and control is exercised, shown by board composition, meeting places and minutes. Permanent establishment: whether a foreign entity has a taxable presence through an office or an agent who signs contracts locally. Treaty entitlement: whether the entity claiming reduced withholding is resident, is the beneficial owner rather than a conduit, and passes anti-abuse tests such as a principal purpose test. Transfer pricing: whether each intercompany fee, interest rate and guarantee fee is at arm's length, with agreements and analysis made at the time. And interest limits: thin-capitalisation or earnings-based caps that can deny interest deductions. Every one of these is decided by evidence, not by the tax rate. So I keep a five-row evidence file for each entity, review it every year, and never assume a treaty applies just because one exists.
terms: Principal purpose test — a treaty anti-abuse rule denying benefits where obtaining them was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement.
Thin capitalisation — a rule limiting interest deductions on debt that is high relative to equity.
Contemporaneous documentation — evidence prepared at the time of a transaction, not reconstructed afterwards.

hostile.q: Your holding company claims treaty-reduced withholding on dividends. What does it actually do with the money it receives?
hostile.a: It decides what to do with it, and here is the record. Its board considers each dividend, retains part to fund the next acquisition, and invested in a second project last year. It is not obliged to pass the income on to anyone. It has its own directors meeting where it is resident, its own bank account and its own decisions, and the reasons for the structure were recorded before it was formed.

title: Tracing a Dollar of Profit Through the Structure
summary: A worked calculation takes hypothetical profit from a project company through fees, interest, local tax, withholding, holding-company tax, conversion and personal tax to the individual at the top. Then it shows what happens when an auditor disallows part of the interest and the fee. The result is the all-in leakage the structure must justify.
body:
The only honest test of a structure is to follow one sum of profit from the building to the person at the top, and count every deduction along the way. Then run it again with the auditor's adjustments, and you know what the structure is really worth.

Recall

Q. How do you reverse engineer the price you need from an asset sale?

A. Start from the net cash you need, gross it up for withholding, add back debt repaid at sale, then undo company tax, selling costs and transfer tax to solve for the price, and check it forward.

Q. What is the value at risk from a narrowed currency gate?

A. The difference between what arrives on the base remittance route and what arrives, in today's money, under rationing and devaluation.

Q. Under a treaty, what usually limits the withholding a source country may charge on dividends?

A. A maximum rate written into the treaty, often lower for a company holding a substantial share of the payer, available only if the recipient is entitled to the treaty's benefits.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an odd week, so we work forward. Every structure in this phase claimed to reduce leakage. A forward trace shows whether it does, and how much of that reduction survives an audit. All numbers are hypothetical, and every rate is an assumption for teaching, not any country's law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The structure and the assumptions

An individual owns a holding company in country A, which owns a project company in country B. The project company earns profit before fees and interest of 3,000,000 dollars. It pays the holding company a management fee of 300,000 dollars and interest of 500,000 dollars on an intercompany loan. Assumptions: country B taxes company profit at 25 percent; withholding in B is 10 percent on fees, 10 percent on interest and 5 percent on dividends under a treaty; country A taxes the holding company at 10 percent on fees and interest, gives a credit for B's withholding, and exempts dividends from qualifying subsidiaries; conversion costs 2 percent; the individual pays 20 percent on dividends received from the holding company.

Step 1: inside the project company

Profit before fees and interest: 3,000,000. Less fee 300,000 and interest 500,000. Taxable profit: 2,200,000. Tax at 25 percent: 550,000. After-tax profit: 1,650,000.

Withholding on the payments upward: 10 percent of 300,000 is 30,000; 10 percent of 500,000 is 50,000. If all after-tax profit is paid as a dividend, withholding at 5 percent is 82,500.

Step 2: inside the holding company

The holding company receives 270,000 of fee, 450,000 of interest and 1,567,500 of dividend: 2,287,500 in total. Tax in A on the fee and interest: 10 percent of 800,000 is 80,000, less a credit for the 80,000 withheld in B, so nothing further. The dividend is exempt. Cash after tax: 2,287,500. Converted at a 2 percent cost: about 2,241,750.

Step 3: to the individual

The holding company pays it all to the individual as a dividend, taxed at 20 percent: about 448,350. The individual keeps about 1,793,400. Total tax and leakage on 3,000,000 of profit: about 1,206,600, or 40.2 percent.

Say that out loud now.

Follow one sum from the building to the person, deduct every layer in order, then run it again with the auditor's adjustments.

Step 4: the auditor's adjustments

Now assume an audit in country B. The auditor accepts only half the management fee as arm's length, for lack of records, and disallows 200,000 of the interest under an interest limit. The project company's taxable profit rises by 150,000 plus 200,000, to 2,550,000. Tax at 25 percent: 637,500, an extra 87,500. Assume a penalty of 20 percent of the extra tax: 17,500. And in country A, the holding company still received and was taxed on the full fee and interest, so no relief arises there unless the two authorities agree a correction, which takes time and is not assured.

After-tax profit in B falls to 3,000,000 less 800,000 of payments less 637,500 of tax less 17,500 of penalty, 1,545,000. Dividend withholding at 5 percent: 77,250. The holding company now receives 270,000 plus 450,000 plus 1,467,750, which is 2,187,750. After conversion: about 2,144,000. After the individual's 20 percent: about 1,715,200.

The individual keeps about 1,715,200 instead of 1,793,400: about 78,200 less, and leakage rises from 40.2 percent to about 42.8 percent. On a single year's profit that is a modest number. Over a ten-year hold, with interest on late tax, and with the risk of the same adjustment in every year, it becomes material, and it is entirely an evidence problem.

Step 5: comparing with no structure

For contrast, assume the individual held the project company directly, with no fees or interest: tax in B of 750,000, dividend withholding to an individual at an assumed 15 percent on 2,250,000, which is 337,500, conversion of about 38,250, and the individual's own tax, assume, at 20 percent less a credit for withholding, about 37,400 more. The individual keeps about 1,836,900. On these assumptions the structure, before audit, leaves the individual less than holding directly, because country A's dividend tax on the individual outweighs the savings in B. That is the point of the exercise: a structure must be traced to the person, not just to the holding company, before anyone claims it saves tax.

Reading the trace honestly

The trace teaches three things that no single lesson in the phase could. First, the largest leak is often not where the planning effort went: here, the individual's own dividend tax in country A outweighed the withholding savings in country B. Second, the audit cost is almost entirely about evidence, not rates: half a fee and part of the interest were lost for want of records and a limit nobody checked. Third, the comparison with direct holding is the only fair benchmark. A structure that leaves you with less money than holding directly must be justified by its other purposes, liability separation, exit flexibility, a services team serving several projects, and those purposes must be written down before it is adopted.

Finally, test sensitivity to the one assumption you trust least. Here it is the individual's dividend tax rate in country A. Run the trace at 15 percent and at 25 percent: on the base case, the individual keeps about 1,905,500 at 15 percent and about 1,681,300 at 25 percent. The structure's verdict against direct holding flips inside that range, which tells you the decision rests on a personal tax question that needs written advice before anything else is formed.

Present the trace to investors and advisers in the same order every time: assumptions, base trace, audit trace, direct-holding comparison, then the non-tax purposes. That order puts the honest numbers before the argument, which is the order a sceptical reader trusts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring a structure's benefit at the holding company, where it looks good, instead of at the individual, where it may not. The control is a forward trace from building to person, run with and without the auditor's likely adjustments, before the structure is adopted.

The beginner's mistake

Counting withholding as an extra tax without checking whether a credit is available, or counting a credit as available without checking that the residence country actually taxes enough to use it.

Callback

In Week 58, Devika and Elias taught that the form of repatriation, dividend, interest, fee or return of capital, decides withholding and leakage. Today's trace is that lesson run through every layer at once, with the auditor's adjustments of Weeks 60 and 61 applied on top.

Recap

Trace one sum of profit from the building to the individual: payments upward, local tax, withholding, holding-company tax and credits, conversion, personal tax. Then apply the auditor's likely adjustments. Compare the result with holding directly. A structure is justified only if it wins at the person, after audit.

Next: Cole, with Priya, on The Room: the full mock meeting, defending a structure chart to an auditor and a banker.
checklist: I trace profit from the building to the individual, every layer.
I list each assumption above the result.
I check whether each withholding is creditable and usable.
I rerun the trace with the auditor's likely adjustments.
I compare the structure with holding the asset directly.
I judge a structure by what reaches the person, not the holding company.
I hold evidence for every fee and interest payment in the trace.
head: Field checklist
speak: I test a structure by following one sum of profit all the way to the person at the top. Hypothetically, a project company earns three million before fees and interest. It pays a fee and interest to its holding company, pays local tax, and withholding applies to each payment upward. The holding company is taxed on the fee and interest with a credit for withholding, its dividend is exempt, conversion costs 2 percent, and the individual pays 20 percent on what comes out. About 1.79 million reaches the individual, leakage near 40 percent. Then I apply the auditor's likely adjustments: half the fee disallowed for lack of records and part of the interest denied under an interest limit. Leakage rises to about 43 percent, entirely because of evidence. And when I compare with holding directly, the structure may not win at all. So I judge a structure by what reaches the person, after audit, not by how it looks at the holding company.
terms: Forward trace — following a sum of profit through every layer of a structure to its final recipient.
Foreign tax credit — relief in the residence country for tax already paid abroad on the same income, usually capped at the residence country's own tax.
Corresponding adjustment — a correction one country may make when another adjusts an intercompany price, to relieve double tax.

hostile.q: You say your structure saves tax. Show me what reaches you personally, before and after a plausible audit.
hostile.a: Here is the forward trace. On these assumptions about 1.79 million of three million reaches me before audit, and about 1.72 million after an auditor disallows half the fee and part of the interest. I have also compared it with holding directly. I am not relying on the structure to save tax; its purpose is to separate liability between projects and to keep exit options open, and I have shown its tax cost honestly.

role: Audit and integrity, with Priya on debt and project finance
title: Mock Meeting: Defending the Chart to an Auditor and a Banker
summary: The full checkpoint mock meeting. You present a hypothetical three-entity structure chart to a tax auditor and a senior banker in the same room. One wants to find profit in the wrong place; the other wants to find cash in the wrong place. Learn to open, answer, concede and close with both listening.
body:
This is the phase in one room. A tax auditor and a banker read the same structure chart for different reasons. Your job is to answer each one completely without giving the other a new problem, and to concede the weak point before either of them finds it.

Recall

Q. What is structural subordination?

A. The position of a lender to a holding company, which is paid only after the subsidiary's creditors, taxes and withholding, because its claim is one step removed from the asset.

Q. In a bank onboarding meeting, what should you do while the compliance officer reads a document?

A. Stay silent. Filling the silence sounds like nerves and invites new questions.

Q. In a treaty negotiation scene, what is the question behind "is your holding company the beneficial owner?"

A. Whether it is a conduit, obliged in law or in practice to pass the income on, or a real owner that decides what to do with it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will rarely meet an auditor and a banker in the same room. You will often meet them in the same month, reading the same documents, and what you tell one becomes evidence for the other. Practising them together forces the discipline that matters: one consistent, evidenced account of your structure.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical facts. Your chart: you own a holding company in country A; it owns a project company in country B that owns a 60-unit building; and a services company in country A provides development management to the project company for a fee. The holding company lent 4,000,000 dollars to the project company. A bank is considering a 12,000,000 dollar refinancing loan to the project company. Around the table: Ms Ade, a tax auditor from country B, reviewing the project company's last three years, and Mr Rowe, the bank's senior credit officer. Priya sits beside you as your finance adviser. Cole, today, is observing the meeting as your coach.

The opening

Say: "Thank you both. I will take ten minutes on the chart, then answer anything. In one sentence: each company has a real purpose, every payment between them is documented and priced, and the bank's loan sits where the cash is. I will also tell you the one place I think the chart is weakest, and what I have done about it."

Naming your weak point in the opening is the most powerful move in this room. It tells the auditor you are not hiding, and it tells the banker you see risk the way it does.

Say that out loud now.

The auditor's questions

Ms Ade asks: "Who decides for the holding company?" The question behind it is residence. Answer with the structure book: "Its board has a majority of directors resident in country A. It met there four times last year. Here are the papers, the minutes and the decisions, including one proposal of mine it declined." Never say "I decide, but they sign." That sentence is Fundy Settlement in one line.

Ms Ade asks: "What does the services company actually do for its fee?" The question behind it is whether the fee is real and at arm's length. Answer: "Development management: budget, procurement, design coordination and lender reporting. Here is the agreement, signed before services began, the monthly reports, the time records and the benchmarking study for the fee." If one year's records are thin, say so now: "For the first year the time records are incomplete. I have the reports and the correspondence, and I would rather you weigh that honestly than find it."

Ms Ade asks: "Is the 4,000,000 loan really debt?" The question behind it is interest limits and recharacterisation. Answer: "It has a written agreement, a market interest rate supported by a pricing note, a fixed repayment schedule that has been met, and it sits within the debt-to-equity limit we were advised applies. Here is the advice."

The banker's questions

Mr Rowe asks: "What ranks ahead of my loan?" Answer with the cash waterfall: "Operating costs, then your debt service. The services fee is capped and subordinated to you. The shareholder loan is subordinated: no interest or principal while anything is owed to you or a covenant is breached. Local tax is paid from income, and I have modelled the auditor's worst plausible adjustment."

Mr Rowe asks: "And if Ms Ade adjusts the fee and the interest?" This is the moment the two readers meet. Answer both at once: "Then the project company pays more tax, which I have modelled at about 90,000 dollars a year in a severe case. Your coverage moves from about 1.40 to 1.35, still above the covenant. The extra tax reduces what goes up to the holding company, not what goes to you." That answer works only because the waterfall puts the bank ahead of the intercompany payments.

The lines never to say

Never tell the auditor the structure exists to reduce tax, and never tell the banker it is "just for tax". Both may be partly true; neither is a purpose that survives scrutiny. State the real purposes: separating liability, holding the services team in one place, keeping exit options. Never give the banker a more favourable account of the fee than you gave the auditor. Never promise the auditor a document you have not seen. And never say "everyone structures it this way."

When to stay silent

When Ms Ade writes, wait. When Mr Rowe looks at the waterfall, wait. When either asks something you do not know, say: "I don't know. I'll confirm in writing by Friday, to both of you," and then do it. A late answer is a delay. An inconsistent answer is a finding.

Holding your state

Two hostile readers at once can feel like being outnumbered. Reframe it before you enter: they want the same thing from you, a consistent account backed by documents. If your pulse rises, slow your speech and lengthen your pauses, a practitioner habit rather than a proven technique. Do any breathing drill beforehand, parked, never while driving.

The close

Say: "To summarise: every entity has a purpose and a record, every payment has an agreement and a price, the bank sits ahead of the intercompany payments, and the one weak year of time records is disclosed. What would each of you need to close your review?" Write both lists. Send one consistent follow-up letter to each, the same day.

Cole's debrief

After the mock meeting, Cole scores three things, and so should you. Consistency: did any answer to the banker contradict an answer to the auditor? Evidence: did every claim end with a document named, or with a promise to confirm in writing? Disclosure: did you name the weak year of time records before Ms Ade reached it? Priya adds a fourth for the banker's side: could you state coverage, before and after the worst plausible adjustment, without looking? Write the four answers down and rerun the scene tomorrow, aloud, with a friend reading the two parts if you can.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is giving two readers two versions. The control is one structure book and one cash waterfall, used for both, and every follow-up checked against the other before it is sent.

The beginner's mistake

Defending the weak point instead of disclosing it. Disclosed, it is a fact being managed. Discovered, it is a reason to doubt everything else.

Callback

In Week 6, you learned to acknowledge, bridge and answer a hostile question, and to say "I'll confirm by Friday" rather than guess. In Week 2, the pre-mortem asked you to find the failure before it happened. Naming your chart's weakest point in the opening is a pre-mortem delivered out loud to the people who would otherwise conduct the post-mortem.

Recap

Open with the bottom line and your weakest point. Answer the auditor with the structure book and the banker with the cash waterfall, and make sure each answer survives the other's question. Never give two versions. Stay silent while they read, confirm unknowns in writing to both, and close with their lists.

Next: Kema's checkpoint: the mock interview, the three-minute recording, and the rules you will not break.
checklist: I open with the bottom line and my structure's weakest point.
I answer residence questions from the structure book.
I answer fee and loan questions with agreements, records and pricing notes.
I answer the banker from a cash waterfall with subordination shown.
I model the auditor's worst plausible adjustment for the banker.
I give the auditor and the banker one consistent account.
I confirm every unknown in writing to both by a stated date.
head: Field checklist
speak: In the mock meeting I defend one structure chart to a tax auditor and a banker at once. I open with the bottom line, that every company has a real purpose, every payment is documented and priced, and the bank's loan sits where the cash is, and I name my weakest point before either finds it. To the auditor's residence question I answer from the structure book: directors, meeting locations, minutes and decisions. To her fee and loan questions I show agreements signed before services, records, pricing notes and the debt-to-equity advice. To the banker I show the cash waterfall: the services fee and shareholder loan are subordinated, so an auditor's adjustment reduces what goes up to my holding company, not what goes to the bank. I never give two versions, never say the structure is just for tax, stay silent while they read, and confirm unknowns in writing to both by Friday.
terms: Consistent account — one version of the structure's purpose and evidence, given identically to every reviewer.
Weak point disclosure — naming the least defensible element of your position before a reviewer finds it.
Pricing note — a short written analysis supporting an intercompany interest rate or fee as arm's length.

hostile.q: You told the bank the services fee is capped and subordinated. You told me it is fully earned and paid monthly. Which is it?
hostile.a: Both, and they are consistent. The fee is earned monthly for services you can see in the reports, and it is accrued monthly. Its payment is capped and subordinated to the bank, so in a month when the bank's conditions are not met, the earned fee is deferred, not cancelled. Here is the agreement clause and the bank's draft subordination agreement; they say the same thing.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: Cross-Border Structure and Tax Strategy
summary: The phase checkpoint. Answer the mock interview aloud, then record a three-minute explanation of the phase on your phone, defending a hypothetical structure chart, and score it 1 to 5 for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.
body:
A phase is learned when you can defend it under pressure, out loud, in three minutes, without notes. Today you find out whether you can defend a cross-border structure to an auditor and a banker, and you write down the score.

Recall

Q. What is a forward trace?

A. Following one sum of profit from the building through every layer of a structure, payments, tax, withholding, credits, conversion and personal tax, to the person at the top.

Q. What does Rule 63 say?

A. Never let my ability to pay depend on a currency promise or bank access I do not control; match debt to the currency of income, keep reserves outside the system I am exposed to, and decide in advance the trigger that makes me move money.

Q. What does relief by credit require before it is worth anything?

A. That the residence country actually taxes the income enough to absorb the credit; a credit against a tax you do not owe saves nothing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this phase is where a developer's wealth is most often lost quietly: not in a crash, but in leakage, adjustments and frozen money that nobody modelled. Reading these lessons builds recognition. Defending a chart aloud builds performance. This checkpoint measures the second, and gives you a score to beat at the next one.

The mock interview

Read each question, answer it aloud before reading the model answer, and be strict with yourself.

Question 1. An auditor asks why your holding company is resident where you say. What do you show her?

Answer: The structure book: a board with resident directors who deliberate, meetings held where the company claims residence, papers sent in advance, minutes that record discussion and decisions, including disagreement. Residence follows the decision-maker, as Fundy Settlement showed in 2012.

Question 2. Your structure pays a management fee, interest and dividends upward. What must each payment have?

Answer: A real legal form, a written agreement made before the payment, an arm's length price supported by analysis, and the correct withholding under domestic law or the treaty, with treaty entitlement and beneficial ownership established.

Question 3. A banker asks what ranks ahead of the loan. What is your answer and why does it matter?

Answer: Lend at the company that owns the building, so only operating costs rank ahead. Subordinate intercompany loans and fees in writing. Otherwise a holding-company lender stands behind tax, fees and withholding, and on hypothetical numbers coverage of 1.33 can fall below one.

Question 4. Why might a lawful structure still be unable to pay you?

Answer: Because money must pass registration, currency rules and a bank. Unregistered capital, rationed currency or a bank that cannot understand the chart can trap profit, as Argentina showed in 2001 and 2002.

Question 5. A buyer offers a headline price. What must be agreed first?

Answer: The form of sale, asset or shares; who bears each tax it creates, including transfer tax, recapture and latent tax; and a current written opinion on its tax. Rule 64.

Question 6. How do you know whether a structure is worth having?

Answer: Trace profit forward to the individual, with and without the auditor's likely adjustments, and compare with holding directly. If it wins only at the holding company, it does not win. Then confirm it has non-tax purposes that survive scrutiny.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Take out your phone, open the voice recorder, and record a three-minute explanation of this phase as if presenting a hypothetical three-entity structure chart to a mock auditor and a banker. Use this structure: what the chart claims, box by box and arrow by arrow; the three ideas, substance follows the decision-maker, form must match flow, and money must be able to move; the five rules an auditor tests; how the bank's loan is protected; and one failure case with its rule. Do not use notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Then listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions, rules and numbers right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip, such as confusing a credit with an exemption.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow the order? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds like someone who has defended charts many times.
  4. The hard question. Did you name your chart's weakest point and what you did about it, unprompted? A 5 raises it before the listener can.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. An example of honest scoring: if you said the holding company is resident because it is registered there, accuracy is a 2, because the phase's central idea is that registration does not decide residence. If you defended the structure by its tax saving rather than its evidence, the hard question is a 2.

What to do with the scores

Act on your lowest score alone this week. If accuracy was lowest, reread the lesson the error came from and rebuild the definition in your own words. If structure was lowest, write the five-part outline on a card and record again tomorrow from the card. If composure was lowest, record again deliberately slower and count filler words. If the hard question was lowest, practise opening with "The weakest point in this chart is..." until it comes first by habit. Record once more at the end of the week and compare. Keep the recordings; at the next checkpoint you will hear the difference.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case, now including Rules 63, 64 and 65. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week. A rule you cannot say from memory will not be there when an adviser offers you a clever structure on a deadline.

A model outline for the recording

If you want a frame before your first attempt, use this, then put it away. One: "This chart makes six claims, and here is the evidence for each." Two: "Three ideas hold it together: substance follows the decision-maker, form must match flow, and money must be able to move." Three: "An auditor will test residence, permanent establishment, treaty entitlement, transfer pricing and interest limits, and this is the file for each." Four: "The bank lends to the company that owns the building, and every intercompany payment is subordinated to it." Five: "The weakest point is one year of thin time records; here is what we did." Six: "The rule I will not break is Rule 65." That is about three minutes spoken at a steady pace. If you finish in under two, you skipped evidence. If you run past four, you explained instead of defending.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading yourself on what you meant rather than what you said. The recording does not care what you meant. Score the tape.

The beginner's mistake

Skipping the recording and reading the model answers instead. Reading feels like mastery and proves nothing. The discomfort of hearing yourself defend a chart is the rehearsal that makes the real meeting familiar.

Callback

In Week 47, the capital phase checkpoint asked you to explain the capital stack and the lender's view. Listen for whether this recording connects the two phases: a structure chart is also a capital stack, and the banker in today's mock meeting is the same lender you met there, now asking where the cash is.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud before reading the answers. Record three minutes defending a hypothetical structure chart, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.

Next: Kema, with JAX, opens the deals and people phase with negotiation: interests versus positions, BATNA, reservation price, anchoring and concessions.
checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: This phase comes down to one idea: a structure chart is a set of claims, and I must be able to prove every one. Three principles carry it. Substance follows the decision-maker: an entity is resident where its real decisions are made, as Fundy Settlement showed in 2012, so I keep a structure book with real boards, real meetings and real minutes. Form must match flow: every fee, loan and dividend has an agreement made in advance, an arm's length price and the right withholding, with treaty entitlement checked. And money must be able to move: registration, currency rules and a bank, as Argentina showed in 2001. An auditor tests residence, permanent establishment, treaty entitlement, transfer pricing and interest limits; a banker tests what ranks ahead of the loan, so I lend where the cash is and subordinate intercompany payments. I trace profit to the person, before and after audit, and I agree the form of sale before the price.
terms: Checkpoint — a scored, recorded performance test of a phase, done without notes.
Decision journal — a dated record of decisions, reasons and scores, reviewed later to measure judgment.
Hard question — the point a hostile listener would raise first, which a strong answer raises before them.

hostile.q: If I removed every tax benefit from your structure, would you still have it?
hostile.a: Yes, in a simpler form, and that is the test I apply. The holding company separates liability between projects and keeps share-sale exits open; the services company keeps one team serving several projects under one contract. Those purposes survive without tax. Where a layer exists only for tax and its evidence is thin, I remove it, and I have shown you the forward trace with and without it.
